title: Conjunction Call
protagonist: Priya Nakamura, satellite operations engineer, Meridian Orbital small-satellite fleet
primary_metric: kilograms of reserve propellant required to cover every real threshold-crossing conjunction predicted this season, compared against the propellant Aurora-7 has left over after reserving enough for her mandatory end-of-mission disposal burn

options.B: Fly The Season -- keep Aurora-7 collecting data through the debris-conjunction season, spending reserve propellant on real avoidance maneuvers only when a conjunction's predicted collision probability crosses the industry threshold

scenario_constructions: Priya Nakamura, Meridian Orbital, and Aurora-7 are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case and Dana Okafor / the Turbine Channel.

Aurora-7's six-event, 45-day conjunction log (Appendix C, MA2) is a stated scenario dataset styled on CelesTrak SOCRATES Plus's real published report format (S4) -- it is not a live feed record for a real, specific satellite.

The 0600 ops-handoff deadline (Overview) is a scenario detail with no real citable source, consistent with the Overview's mid-crisis framing, disclosed as a stated scenario detail rather than sourced externally.

balance.argument_a: De-Orbit Now is certain and immediately compliant: zero propellant risk, a guaranteed-clean disposal burn spent now while there is unambiguously enough fuel to do it, and no exposure to any conjunction this case's own numbers might have gotten wrong. Even though the Challenge D1-D4 arithmetic shows Fly The Season's propellant math technically works out, it leaves only a thin cushion (computed margin below SPEC's 20% cap) after this season's real threshold-crossing maneuvers -- one larger-than-predicted maneuver, or one more flagged event than Appendix C shows, and Aurora-7 could be left without enough propellant to complete the same mandatory disposal burn Option A completes with certainty today.
balance.argument_b: Fly The Season wins on this case's actual computed primary metric. Using the real NASA CARA 1e-4 threshold (S1) to determine which of Appendix C's six events actually require a maneuver, and the real Busek BIT-3 specific impulse (S3) to convert each maneuver's delta-v into a propellant mass, Aurora-7's season of real threshold-crossing maneuvers costs 0.01195 kg -- comfortably inside the 0.0140 kg she has available after reserving MA5's mandatory 0.0100 kg disposal minimum, leaving a real, computed 14.64% propellant cushion. Forty-five more days of already-funded, still-working ocean-color data is a real asset to give up for a risk that the numbers, as currently predicted, show is affordably covered.
balance.margin_basis: Total propellant required for every Appendix C event whose maximum Pc crosses the real S1 threshold (1e-4): events E2, E4, E5, E6, total delta-v 21.0 m/s. Propellant per m/s = wet mass (MA3, 12.0 kg) / (Isp (S3, 2,150 s) x g0 (9.80665 m/s^2)) = 12.0 / 21,084.30 = 5.691e-4 kg per m/s. Total propellant required = 21.0 x 5.691e-4 = 0.011951 kg. Propellant available for avoidance = total reserve (MA4, 0.024 kg) - mandatory disposal reserve (MA5, 0.0100 kg) = 0.0140 kg. margin_pct = (0.0140 - 0.011951) / 0.0140 x 100 = 14.64%. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.
balance.twist_effect: Under the twist (a 7th conjunction event, Pc 6.0e-4, required delta-v 5.5 m/s, day 44), total propellant required becomes 21.0+5.5=26.5 m/s worth, i.e. 0.015081 kg, against the same 0.0140 kg available -- a shortfall of about 0.001081 kg. The pre-twist 14.64% cushion (winner B) is fully consumed and the winner flips to A under sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist(): base {A:0.0, B:45.0}, twist {A:0.0, B:-1.0}. Verified by re-deriving under the case's own stated Appendix D arithmetic, not a different convention.

A propellant-budget table deriving kilograms of propellant required per meter/second of delta-v from Aurora-7's thruster's real specific impulse and stated wet mass, then computing the total propellant cost of every avoidance maneuver Challenge D2 shows is really required.

A decision memo comparing Option A's certain outcome against Option B's outcome computed from D1-D3, including the propellant Aurora-7 must still have left over afterward for her mandatory disposal burn, with a stated recommendation and supporting arithmetic.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: reserve_propellant_kg (MA4, 0.024 kg) is a good-faith scenario estimate for a fictional, aging, low-fuel satellite -- not a publicly documented fuel state for any real satellite, since no such per-satellite figure is ever publicly disclosed. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep confirms this is genuinely load-bearing: at -50% (0.012 kg) the available-for-avoidance pool shrinks to 0.0020 kg, far below the 0.011951 kg required, flipping the recommendation to A; at +50% (0.036 kg) the available pool grows to 0.0260 kg, widening the cushion well past comfortable. This is disclosed in full -- MA4 is the single most fragile, dilemma-relevant assumption in the case, and a Hero who challenges this specific figure is raising exactly the right question.

disposal_reserve_kg (MA5, 0.0100 kg) is a good-faith scenario estimate of a disposal-compliance minimum for a fictional operator's fictional policy -- no public per-mission figure exists, since the real number depends on the specific spacecraft/thruster/target-orbit combination, none of which are standardized or published for a fictional case. Shares MA4's propellant pool, so it moves the same feasibility check: +50% (0.0150 kg) shrinks the available pool to 0.0090 kg, below the 0.011951 kg required, flipping to A; -50% (0.0050 kg) widens the pool to 0.0190 kg. Disclosed for the same reason as MA4 -- a Hero who challenges this figure is raising exactly the right question.

wet_mass_kg (MA3, 12.0 kg) is a good-faith scenario estimate consistent with the BIT-3 thruster's real published reference-platform mass class (S3, a 14 kg 6U CubeSat) -- no real published mass exists for the fictional Aurora-7. It scales the propellant-per-m/s conversion factor directly: at +50% (18.0 kg) the per-maneuver propellant cost rises enough to exceed the 0.0140 kg available, flipping to A; at -50% (6.0 kg) it falls well under, widening the cushion. Disclosed in full; not eliminated by retuning, because 12.0 kg is itself the case's honest best-effort estimate, not an arbitrary dial.

total_maneuver_dv_ms (the sum of MA2's four maneuvering events' stated delta-v, 21.0 m/s) is part of Appendix C's disclosed scenario conjunction log -- a specific per-event delta-v history for a fictional satellite's fictional season has no real-world source to cite. At +50% (31.5 m/s) required propellant exceeds the 0.0140 kg available, flipping to A; at -50% (10.5 m/s) the cushion widens well past comfortable. This is the same instability the Twist (case.json.facilitator.twist / balance.twist_effect) demonstrates directly and concretely inside the case's own discussion, rather than only in an abstract +/-50% sweep -- both point at the same real fragility: the season's real conjunction count and required delta-v are not fully known in advance.

facilitator.twist: A seventh conjunction event is discovered mid-discussion: a newly-cataloged fragment from an unrelated collision, screened for the first time this morning, with a maximum Pc of 6.0e-4 and a required avoidance delta-v of 5.5 m/s -- arriving on day 44, after Aurora-7 has already spent propellant on E2/E4/E5/E6.

catalog.ask: Priya's small-satellite fleet has a season of predicted close approaches with other objects in orbit. Fly every maneuver NASA's own collision-risk threshold recommends, burning through reserve propellant fast, or fly the season and accept the miss-distance risk on the ones that look safest? The numbers are all in scientific notation, and the difference between them is the whole decision.

context_glossary.desc: Satellite-operator word for two tracked objects predicted to pass unusually close together. Nothing to do with the grammar term.
A real, free public report that lists every predicted close approach between orbiting objects, refreshed three times a day.
A small electric engine that pushes a satellite by accelerating charged particles instead of burning chemical fuel. Very efficient, but very gentle.
Engineers' measure of how big a maneuver is: the change in velocity it needs, whatever the spacecraft's mass.
An orbit shaped so the satellite crosses any given spot on Earth at the same local time every day, handy for comparing images day to day.
